title: The letter A may have started out as a picture of an ox’s head
body: The earliest known ancestor of A is **aleph**, the first letter of the Phoenician alphabet, whose name comes from the West Semitic word for ox. Its shape goes back to a Proto-Sinaitic sign that *may* have pictured an ox’s head, borrowed from Egyptian hieroglyphs; the oldest examples of that script, scratched on rocks, date to about 1850 BC. Phoenician wrote only consonants, so aleph stood for a catch in the throat, a glottal stop. Greek had no such sound, so the Greeks used the sign for the vowel a and called it alpha; set upright, it passed through the Etruscans to the Romans, and on to us.

slides.heading: Match each Phoenician letter to its meaning
slides.explanation: Each letter’s name was a word that began with its sound: bet for b, mem for m, kap for k. Alp began with a glottal stop.

slides.alt: Animation: a capital A carved in sandstone turns upside down and grows horns, becoming an ox-head sign. It turns on its side as Phoenician aleph, becomes Greek alpha in ink on papyrus, stands upright and ends as a printed A beside a B that grew from a house sign.

slides.prompt: Slide through time and watch the ox-head sign become A. Then follow the house sign to B.
slides.takeaway: A is an ox head turned on its side by the Phoenicians and set upright later; B grew from a house sign. Each sign stood for the first sound of its word: alp, ox; bet, house.

slides.heading: Named for its first sound
slides.text: The first alphabet’s signs probably stood for the first sound of the word for what they showed. The house sign, Semitic *bayt*, came to write b and became the ancestor of our B.

slides.heading: Why “may”?
slides.text: The ox’s head is a scholarly reconstruction. Proto-Sinaitic has not been fully deciphered, and the Egyptian models for its signs are hypotheses, with several possibilities proposed.

slides.question: Why did the Greeks turn aleph into a vowel?
options: Phoenician aleph was already a vowel
slides.explanation: Phoenician wrote only consonants, and aleph was a glottal stop. Greek had no use for that sound, so the sign was used for the vowel a and named alpha.

slides.heading: The word itself
slides.text: *Alphabet* comes from Greek alpha and beta, whose names came from the first two Phoenician letters: aleph, the word for ox, and bet, the word for house.
